title: Where did it go wrong for Russell – and can he regroup for 2027?
excerpt:
The stadium at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is a superb sporting stage. When it’s the scene of a champion's coronation the atmosphere becomes truly special – as we witnessed on Sunday for Kimi Antonelli.

Five minutes after the chequered flag waved in Mexico City, George Russell ventured into the great spectacle, surveying what he could have won.

The ticker tape was fluttering down upon the cars and the trio of title winning drivers on the podium. The black and gold World Champion board was placed at the nose of a silver Mercedes – but not his.

title: When could Mercedes win the 2026 Teams' Championship?
excerpt:
Mercedes head to Brazil this weekend with a real possibility of sealing the Teams' Championship title. The Silver Arrows lead the standings by 126 points from Ferrari after a double points finish in Mexico City.

Kimi Antonelli has already wrapped up the Drivers' Championship, winning last weekend courtesy of his P3 finish at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

But what does his team have to do to win the other crown at Interlagos, or will the title fight rumble on to the final triple-header?

How many points are still up for grabs?

There are four rounds remaining in the 2026 season, so a maximum of 172 points remain up for grabs if a team records a 1-2 at every Grand Prix.

No team has got close to doing that this season, with Mercedes recording back-to-back 1-2 finishes in the first two rounds and again in Monza.

Ferrari have only had both drivers on the same rostrum once, at Silverstone.

Which teams are still in contention for the title?

Mercedes lead the way, with Ferrari the only team who can still catch them. Both Red Bull and McLaren have dropped out of the fight.

Mercedes have scored 630 points so far in 2026, with Antonelli taking nine Grand Prix wins and George Russell three.

Ferrari have ammassed 504 points, but they have only bagged two Grand Prix victories - one for Lewis Hamilton in Barcelona, and one for Charles Leclerc at Silverstone.

Despite Max Verstappen's late season form, winning three of the last four races, Red Bull are too far back and have already dropped out of contention.

Teams' standings after the Mexico City Grand Prix

When can Mercedes win the title?

Mercedes had a slim chance of winning both titles in Mexico City, but they needed an unlikely set of results to clinch the Teams' Championship last weekend.

However, in Brazil they have a bigger chance. If they leave Interlagos more than 128 points ahead of Ferrari, they will have done enough to take the title. There will be 129 points left on the table after this weekend, but given Mercedes have won more races, in the event of a tie they would win on countback.

With a lead of 126 points already, Mercedes do not need to do much to clinch the title next weekend. They simply need to outscore Ferrari by three points or more.

If Ferrari fail to score, an eighth-place finish for either Antonelli or Russell would be enough for Mercedes to seal the title, while a Ferrari 1-2 would guarantee the championship battle continues beyond Brazil.

If Ferrari win the race, Mercedes can still clinch the title if Antonelli and Russell finish high enough up the order, provided the other Ferrari finishes lower down.

Should Mercedes fail to secure the crown at Interlagos, their next opportunity will come at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, before the season concludes in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

title: Camara concedes ‘there is a lot to learn’ ahead of F1 debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has admitted that “there is a lot to learn” as he prepares to drive a 2026 Formula 1 car for the first time at this weekend’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the Brazilian replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas.

Reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa had been drafted into the American squad last time out in Mexico City, but with a World Endurance Championship finale to contest, he is to step aside for Camara to make his debut at his home event.

While Haas had previously confirmed that the Ferrari junior – who is currently leading the F2 standings – will race for them next season, they have brought his first race forward before he takes on the full-time driver role.

Addressing the opportunity, Camara said in the team's weekend preview: “I’m grateful to TGR Haas F1 Team for giving me this opportunity, and I also want to thank Ferrari for their continued support.

“Making my Formula 1 debut in Brazil is a special moment for me. I know there is a lot to learn, and my focus is on working closely with the team, understanding the car and doing the best job I can this weekend.”

Upon the news of Camara’s 2027 contract, Team Principal Ayao Komatsu explained that the 21-year-old had shown impressive pace during a two-day test in Haas’ 2025 challenger at Portimao, convincing him of the rookie’s speed and ability to handle pressure.

That prior experience will help to an extent when he competes alongside his new team mate and fellow Ferrari-backed driver Ollie Bearman, with the Briton hopeful to maximise Haas’ potential after frustrating back-to-back retirements in the United States and Mexico.

There’s also a sense of history repeating itself for Bearman as he similarly made a late appearance for the team at the Sao Paulo venue in 2024, albeit with multiple FP1 runs and two Grands Prix already under his belt.

“This triple header hasn’t been too kind to me so far, we’ve had promising pace, but I’m yet to cross a finish line,” he said. “I’ll be ending that streak this weekend in São Paulo, and what a track to have a great result on with the history and the fans – this city has it all.

“I’ve raced for the team here twice already, subbing in for Kevin [Magnussen] in 2024, so I know a little about how Rafa will be feeling. The focus is to work together to get some points for the team as we head into the business end of the season.”

title: Rosberg opens up on Hamilton relationship after retirement
excerpt:
Nico Rosberg and Lewis Hamilton shared one of the most intense and memorable rivalries in F1 history, so it’s perhaps not surprising that the German believes they still won’t “be best friends” a decade after the “crazy intense” 2016 season.

The pair had competed alongside one another since their karting days, but their relationship unravelled over four seasons as Mercedes team mates between 2013 and 2016, during which Hamilton won two titles and Rosberg clinched one.

Their tumultuous partnership in that final year produced multiple costly clashes, such as at the Austrian and Spanish Grands Prix, but Rosberg ultimately secured his sole Drivers’ Championship by five points over the Briton.

He went on to announce his shock retirement from the sport just five days after his triumph, opening the door for Valtteri Bottas to join the Silver Arrows for the 2017 season and beyond.

“I apologise to all the fans at the time who wanted to see that fight go on because it was a great battle between Lewis and I,” Rosberg shared on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid. “I'd given it my all and achieved my dream, and to go out on a high is something really valuable for the rest of my life.

“In hindsight, it was the right decision thankfully – I didn't know at the time. It was scary. It was very scary, but it was right for me. I could not have got better. I was at the peak, I know that.

“For me, [another season] was going to be tough because I just threw everything at [2016] – more than everything, and it was crazy intense. It was not really realistic to keep up that level year in, year out.”

He explained that while Team Principal Toto Wolff accepted that his decision was “definitive”, Non-Executive Chairman and former World Champion Niki Lauda was “more on the angry side” due to the position it left Mercedes in.

“I was compromising their team, unfortunately,” Rosberg admitted. “They now have to find a replacement and there was nobody there initially. That's why I decided on telling them so quickly and announcing my retirement so quickly – it was only for the team.

The top 10 driver/team combination wins in F1 history

“I would have preferred to do one month celebrating and then after one month say, ‘Oh, by the way, I'm going to end it here.’

"That would have been much nicer, because the retirement almost became a bigger thing afterwards than my winning, actually. For me, that was not optimal, but it didn't matter.

“The most important thing was to reduce how much I'm compromising the team, and not make it even worse unnecessarily. I wanted to tell them immediately, as quickly as possible so that they could have time to replace and rebuild.”

Although he still mingles in the F1 world, primarily as a pundit, Rosberg has no regrets about his retirement from racing and remains satisfied that he was able to go out on the high of being crowned champion – even if Hamilton made it a challenge at the season finale.

Reflecting on that momentous day in Abu Dhabi, Rosberg said: “Of course, he’s always gracious in those moments.

“Just like I also congratulated him when he won the championship and told him that it was deserved, you know, and then he congratulated me as well. It was a hard one, though, because he didn't obey the team orders. He was bunching us up.

“It triggered the risk that the team would lose the race win because there's [Sebastian] Vettel and [Max] Verstappen coming up from behind, and it's very clear that he's driving slowly on purpose, very slowly.

“It’s understandable in the situation that you're not just going to hand it to me at that moment and you try and keep it in the grey area and keep playing the game.

“For me now, in hindsight, it’s amazing that he did that because it just became all the nicer. It was horrible in the moment.”

Asked whether his relationship with Hamilton improved after his retirement, he replied: “Of course. Anything will thaw after that. It's fine now, it’s neutral.”

He rejected a comparison of their situation to that of Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost following the latter’s sabbatical in 1992, adding: “Maybe not to that extent I think because they really became friends, in a weird way.

“We're just neutral and it's okay, it's nice. We will just not be best friends ever, you know?”

title: The 5 drivers most likely to qualify fastest in Brazil
excerpt:
Max Verstappen may have won three of the last four races, including wins in the Bahrain, Singapore and Mexico City Grand Prix, but he was not able to secure pole position in all three races as Qualifying continues to provide a varied list of winners in 2026.

Lewis Hamilton picked up his first pole of the season in Mexico ahead of George Russell and Charles Leclerc, but the race was won by Verstappen, who qualified fourth and started fifth after being handed a one-place grid penalty.

In total, six different drivers have taken pole over the last seven rounds, with only Verstappen being a repeat winner, in Sepang and Singapore.

There is a slightly different look to the betting markets for Qualifying in Brazil, with the Ferrari duo of Hamilton and Leclerc given a better chance of taking pole than winning the actual race, while the fifth driver in the market is different to the race odds, with oddsmakers preferring the chances of Russell over Lando Norris.

Our expert betting writers have looked at the Qualifying odds and assessed the chances of the leading contenders for pole at Interlagos.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Verstappen has been favourite for pole at the last two races in the United States and Mexico City but qualified only second and fourth-fastest in those races.

That hasn't stopped bookmakers from putting him at the top of the market for Qualifying again this week, and he is the same price that he was to grab pole in Mexico at 6/4 (2.50, +150).

Verstappen now has more wins than poles this season, but while his 2024 Sao Paulo success came from an unpromising starting position of 17th, his 2019 and 2023 victories there were both achieved from pole.

Sao Paulo Grand Prix race betting guide

Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)

Kimi Antonelli took pole at six of the first 10 races this season, but since then he has been the fastest qualifier once which was in Austin, Texas.

Bookmakers are not prepared to take any chances with the newly-crowned World Champion and have made him the second-favourite for pole in Brazil at 5/2 (3.50, +250).

The Italian ace already has experience of two Qualifying sessions at this track, and went second-fastest to Norris in both the Sprint and Grand Prix last season.

Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

Ferrari took their first pole of the season in Mexico City through Hamilton and there is little between their drivers in the Qualifying betting this week with both on offer at 5/1 (6.0, +500).

Leclerc was close in Q3 last week, taking third place on the grid, which followed his second place finish in Qualifying in Singapore and a disappointing fourth in Austin, where he had gone fastest in Q2.

The Monegasque driver has never taken pole at this track but he has been competitive in Qualifying in recent years, taking second in 2023 and setting the third-fastest time last season.

The 5 drivers most likely to win in Brazil

Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)

Hamilton increased his tally of career pole positions to 105 with his success in Mexico City, and he has been given the same odds as Leclerc to be fastest in Qualifying this week, having been available at bigger odds than his team mate to take pole at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Hamilton first took pole at Interlagos back in 2012 for McLaren and has also qualified fastest there for Mercedes in 2016 and 2018, although he had a tough time in Qualifying at this track last season, failing to reach Q3 in both Sprint Qualifying where he was 11th and Grand Prix Qualifying where he was 13th.

George Russell (Mercedes)

Russell is only sixth in the Grand Prix betting markets for Interlagos but he is ahead of Norris in the betting market for Qualifying at 12/1 (13.0, +1200) to take his first pole since Azerbaijan.

He has been the fastest qualifier five times this season and pulled out a great Q3 lap to earn a front-row start in Mexico before having deployment issues on the first lap of the race.

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The 2026 F1 season marches on this weekend with the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, held at the ever-entertaining Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

For this year's event, the C3 has been selected as the hard compound, with the C4 as the medium and C5 as the soft. This marks a shift towards the softer end of the range compared to last season, when Pirelli offered the C2, C3 and C4 over what was a Sprint weekend.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The Brazilian circuit features several changes compared to last season," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "During the year, resurfacing work was carried out on the section between Turns 3 and 5 and between Turns 8 and 9.

"These newly surfaced areas could alter grip levels and track evolution over the course of the weekend, particularly affecting tyre behaviour over longer runs. The three free practice sessions will provide an opportunity to assess track evolution and understand how the new surface influences degradation and wear.

"Twelve months ago, tyre degradation was one of the key technical factors in Sao Paulo. Although graining was less pronounced than initially expected, the C2 compound (used as the hard tyre that year) showed some tendency to slide, while the C3 and C4 displayed significant degradation, albeit still allowing competitive stints. The most effective strategy proved to be a two-stop race.

"In terms of tyre loads, Interlagos generates overall lateral forces that are broadly average, while combining several high-speed corners with long straights. The layout therefore does not place extreme demands on the tyres, with loads distributed fairly evenly between the front and rear axles.

"The numerous overtaking opportunities offered by the circuit’s flowing layout give teams a degree of strategic flexibility, but managing degradation traditionally remains the key factor in maximising race performance. Finding the right balance between single-lap pace and tyre management over longer stints will be one of the main objectives of the teams’ trackside work during the Brazilian weekend.

"It is also worth remembering that, because of the event’s position in the calendar, Interlagos is a circuit where rain and significant temperature fluctuations are often a factor. Intermediate and full wet tyres could therefore come into play in Brazil once again this year."

For more information about Pirelli’s F1 tyres, visit pirelli.com.

title: What is the weather forecast for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix?
excerpt:
Brazil hosts Round 20 of the 2026 season, with the drivers and teams heading to Sao Paulo for the final part of this triple header.

But what kind of weather conditions will the Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace - better known as Interlagos - see this weekend?

Brazil so often gives the world of F1 wet weather classics, but last year the race was run in the dry, with Lando Norris winning for McLaren. He beat Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen in what was a still a chaotic race with Safety Cars and crashes featuring on Sunday afternoon.

Norris might be in the mix again this year, while Antonelli and Verstappen certainly will be. Those two look set to fight with the Ferraris, as everyone watches on to see how Antonelli will drive in the wake of sealing his maiden Drivers' title.

Scroll down for a more detailed look at the forecast for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend weather forecast

FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 06 – FP1 AND FP2

Conditions: The weather is expected to be cloudy and mostly dry, with a high of 25.5°C and a low of 18°C. Morning fog may occur, especially if plentiful rain occurs the day before. Winds will be gentle, averaging 9 km/h with occasional gusts up to 30 km/h. There's a 30% chance of precipitation expected during the early morning and again at night, with track temperatures reaching around 45°C during the afternoon given ample sunshine. Overall, conditions should be favourable for the initial practice sessions, but will have to watch for an isolated shower.

Maximum temperature expected: 25 Celsius

Minimum temperature expected: 18 Celsius

Chance of rain: 30%

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 07 – FP3 AND QUALIFYING

Conditions: Expect warm and partly cloudy conditions, with temperatures ranging from 15°C to 27.5°C. Light to moderate winds could peak at 25 km/h, while non-thunderstorm gusts might reach up to 50 km/h. There's a 50% chance of rain, but if rain does occur it could be significant. The favoured timing for precipitation at this range is after 1400 on Saturday, with precipitation potentially lingering through the evening. Localised urban flooding and standing water at the track will be possible. Track temperature may peak near 40°C, but could trend higher if less cloud cover is observed during the afternoon.

Maximum temperature expected: 27 Celsius

Minimum temperature expected: 15 Celsius

Chance of rain: 50%

SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 08 – RACE

Conditions: The weather on race day is expected to be cool and potentially unsettled again. Temperatures will range from 13°C to 19°C, with a 40% chance of heavy rain and thunderstorms. Winds will be moderate, with average speeds of 15 km/h and gusts reaching up to 40 km/h. The track temperature should peak near 30°C, given the ample cloud cover expected. The clouds and post-frontal air mass should help keep conditions cool through the period, leading to no heat hazard concerns.

Maximum temperature expected: 19 Celsius

Minimum temperature expected: 13 Celsius

Chance of rain: 40%

title: Sergio Perez addresses second Cadillac F1 seat scrutiny as Colton Herta rumours persist
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has insisted he is not having any say in who lines up alongside him at Cadillac next year.

Ahead of last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, Cadillac announced it had secured the services of Perez until at least the end of the 2029 season.

However, there is believed to be further doubt over Valtteri Bottas' drive, despite the Finn joining on what was communicated as a multi-year deal.

Cadillac has been pushing for Herta to obtain his super licence, which he can do this weekend in Brazil during FP1, needing 24 laps to rack up the necessary mileage to secure the 40th point that's required to race in F1.

But Perez highlighted that he is leaving all of the decisions up to team boss Marcin Budkowski.

"No, not at all. I don't want to, either, because that's not my decision," Perez told media including RacingNews365.

"That's why we have someone like Marcin, who will be looking at all the data and information, and he will ultimately make that decision based on what he thinks is best for the future of the team.

"Obviously, we're in a period where we need to evolve extremely quickly. The next three or four months are really crucial in our preparation. So, yeah, I think it's down to him."

[Article continues below]

Herta doing 'good job' for Cadillac, says Perez

Herta made the switch to Formula 2 this year as he targeted a promotion to F1 in 2027, but the campaign has not gone as hoped.

With just five point-scoring finishes, Herta sits 19th in the drivers' championship.

However, Perez has asserted that the American's contribution on the F1 side has been valuable for Cadillac.

"He's doing a good job," he said. "He's bringing good feedback to the team and good information, which is all we need from him.

"Obviously, doing FP1s is always very difficult to show your speed or the level you're at. But now I think he's having more time in the car and in the simulator, so we're starting to see more of his speed.

"Obviously, it's not my decision, but I think it will be down to Marcin to decide who they want in the car. I'm also working really well with Valtteri.

"He's been very unfortunate in a few races. There isn't an easy decision for the team."

title: Formula E legend 'clock was ticking' as Envision prepared for fresh start
excerpt:
Envision was one of the first teams on the Formula E grid to confirm its driver pairing for the upcoming season, with it taking on an entirely new duo.

Paysafe Envision team principal Sylvain Filippi has revealed the squad had long anticipated Sebastien Buemi's departure from its full-time Formula E line-up, with the Swiss driver's World Endurance Championship commitments making his exit all but inevitable.

Buemi, who spent twelve years in the all-electric series, stepped down from his race seat at the end of the 2025/26 campaign to focus on his programme with Toyota Gazoo Racing in WEC.

He has been retained by Envision in an advisory and development capacity heading into the Gen4 era, and tested Jaguar's Gen4 car earlier this year.

Filippi said the timing had become unavoidable given the growing demands of both championships, with each announcing longer calendars than in previous years.

"We knew with Seb the clock was ticking," Filippi told RacingNews365 during an interview. "There was only a point up to which Formula E could keep adding races, and even WEC is adding races now, so we knew that at some point this wasn't going to last forever because it's just not possible, really.

"To my sadness, because it is so easy and great to work with Seb. So, yeah, we've been preparing for this for a while, really. And there's also this kind of rhythm every few years where you need fresh blood coming into a championship, right?

"It might stabilise for a few years, but there are phases where some drivers retire, leave or do something else, or typically WEC or Formula E becomes too much, so at some point you need fresh blood.

"So, when you do, you want to make sure you're as well prepared as possible, which was basically our thinking. We wanted to avoid putting someone new in a car who is kind of new to everything."

Envision not embarking on complete 'new chapter'

That preparation came in the form of Zak O'Sullivan, who joined Envision as a simulator and development driver back in January 2025 and has since completed rookie and test outings at Jeddah, Berlin, Miami and Madrid.

The Briton, a 2021 GB3 champion who also claimed feature race wins at Monaco and Spa-Francorchamps in Formula 2 last year, has now been signed to a multi-year deal alongside Maximilian Günther who has joined from DS Penske.

To welcome two new drivers, Envision also said goodbye to Joel Eriksson after one season.

Filippi insists the arrival of two new drivers does not amount to a full reset for Envision, pointing instead to the stability built around them.

Asked if the upcoming season feels like a new chapter for Envision, Filippi replied: "Yes and no. It does in some respects. Having said that, the rest of the team is so stable.

"The drivers are really the new faces. Apart from that, the team is growing slowly but surely, but not at a crazy rate. We have a cost cap anyway, so we can't really do much more.

"We are cost-cap limited now, but the rest of the team is very, very stable. So, in a sense, it's very much continuity. But, yeah, in terms of drivers, it's really the ideal time to bring new drivers in, right? Because everybody starts from scratch."

Envision recently completed a successful shakedown at Silverstone, with both cars and drivers being used.

title: Ferrari 'management failure' prompts Fred Vasseur scolding: 'You need a ruthless leader'
excerpt:
Ferrari has been told the tension generated between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in Mexico City last weekend was the result of "management failure" within the team.

The duo were battling for the lead on the opening lap last Sunday, with Leclerc attacking Hamilton in a move that saw them go side-by-side through Turn 4.

Both drivers ran off the track, allowing Max Verstappen to slip through ahead of Hamilton, and eventually ahead of Leclerc for the lead when the Monegasque driver was issued a five-second time penalty for gaining an advantage off the track.

Hamilton vented his anger after the grand prix, with Verstappen going on to seal the win for Red Bull.

It did not mark the first time this year that the Ferrari drivers have come to blows, as at its home round at Monza in September, Hamilton was pushed wide and into the gravel on the opening lap by Leclerc.

When asked if Ferrari should have enforced racing rules between their drivers from the beginning of their stint together, former F1 driver Derek Daly exclusively told RacingNews365: "Yes.

"It was a management failure on behalf of Ferrari. Go back to their most successful days with [Michael] Schumacher and Jean Todt calling the shots.

"Jean Todt was a lot more ruthless than Fred Vasseur [Ferrari team principal], and in the situation you have right now, you need a ruthless leader. I have yet to see Fred Vasseur become a ruthless leader."

[Article contines below]

Ferrari boss warned of 'major problem' going forward

Hamilton joined Ferrari last year after bringing the curtain down on his successful stint with Mercedes, where he won six titles to establish himself as the most successful driver in the sport's history.

Having partnered up with Leclerc, who has been part of the Ferrari set-up for some time, Daly believes Vasseur's hands are tied when it comes to team orders.

"Fred Vasseur has a major issue on his hands," he said. "There is no way he can suggest to Charles Leclerc, 'I want you to give way to Lewis more often'.

"And there's no way he's going to be able to go to Lewis and say, 'I want you to give way'."

Ferrari has not been able to consistently challenge at the front of the field this year, with Mercedes already clinching the drivers' title, while it also sits on the verge of the constructors' championship.

While Daly believes Ferrari has gained commercially by Hamilton joining, he insisted it traded away car development when it closed the door on Carlos Sainz.

"Lewis is at the end of his career," Daly said. "There are very few opportunities left to win races. Lewis can almost get into a desperate situation.

"Part of the fascination of F1 is, how do you manage these star names? I don't think it's easy, but remember, Lewis' greatest days are behind him.

"Ferrari, as a team, need to be careful that the power of the marketing machine that is Lewis Hamilton isn't detrimental to the growth and development from an engineering standpoint of the team and of the cars.

"Lewis is not the feedback driver that George Russell is or that Carlos Sainz is. They took the marketing machine, and their marketing machine is bigger than ever, but they sacrificed, I believe, car development."

title: Who is Rafael Camara? The F1 rookie set for baptism of fire
excerpt:
Rafael Camara will make his F1 race debut this weekend at his home grand prix in Sao Paulo, with Haas confirming the Brazilian will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the Interlagos weekend alongside Oliver Bearman.

The move comes sooner than planned, as Camara had already signed a multi-year deal with Haas to join the team full-time from 2027.

But Ocon's permanent removal from the seat, following internal disputes during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, has fast-tracked his arrival by more than a year.

Last weekend, it was Ryo Hirakawa who deputised for Ocon - however, the Japanese driver is unavailable for Brazil due to a scheduling clash with the World Endurance Championship finale at Monza.

But just who is Camara, and how has the 21-year-old found himself in position to race in F1?

[Article continues below]

Camara facing major debut obstacle

Camara arrives on the F1 grid with a formidable junior record. He won the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship with Prema before claiming the FIA Formula 3 title in his rookie season with Trident in 2025, sealing that championship with a round to spare on the back of four feature-race wins and a category-record five poles.

This year, racing for Invicta in Formula 2, he has taken three victories and seven podiums from 25 starts, amassing 207 points to lead the championship standings.

But none of that experience will make Sunday straightforward. A home debut at Interlagos carries weight few circuits on the calendar can match, and no doubt his entry will capture the attention of the local fans who will have a second Brazilian to cheer for.

To further complicate the situation, the conditions are set to be far from ideal.

Friday practice is expected to be overcast with highs near 24°C, but Saturday brings a sharp jump to around 29°C alongside a 60 to 70 per cent chance of thunderstorms disrupting qualifying. Sunday swings the other way entirely, with temperatures dropping to roughly 17°C and a 40 to 50 per cent rain risk lingering into the race start.

Throughout the years, there have been some major shunts at Interlagos - including last year for Gabriel Bortoleto - and any such moment for Camara would be a big stain on what is set to be the biggest weekend of his career to date.

Whether Camara retains the seat beyond this weekend remains unclear, with his ongoing F2 commitments raising questions over whether he or Hirakawa will take the Haas for the season's final rounds in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

title: Why Mercedes' W17 was the perfect weapon for historic Kimi Antonelli F1 title triumph
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli secured the 2026 Formula 1 drivers' world championship in Mexico City, becoming the first Italian to claim the title since Alberto Ascari 73 years earlier.

That statistic alone underlines the scale of the achievement by the 20-year-old from Bologna, who found the ideal partner in his Mercedes W17.

More than simply a competitive car, it became the instrument with which Antonelli produced what can justifiably be described as a masterpiece.

But how good was the W17? Was it an overwhelmingly dominant machine, or an exceptionally strong car that was nevertheless far from perfect — and, crucially, difficult to extract the maximum performance from?

The answer lies in Mercedes' unconventional development philosophy and Antonelli's remarkable ability to exploit the car's strengths while working around its limitations.

[Article continues below]

Mercedes took a different approach to developing the W17

The W17 had already made a strong impression during pre-season testing, although much of the attention focused on the performance of the power unit developed at Mercedes' Brixworth facility rather than any particular advantage in aerodynamics, chassis design or suspension.

What was less immediately apparent was just how advanced the W17's overall concept already was.

Mercedes' technical team, led by James Allison, had approached the project with the conviction that the power unit would form the foundation around which the entire car should be designed.

That belief prompted an unusual development strategy, one that ran counter to both conventional practice and the approach Mercedes expected its rivals to adopt.

Ahead of the season, the widespread assumption throughout the paddock was that teams would introduce a steady stream of upgrades as they developed their understanding of the new generation of cars.

That proved to be the case for almost everyone — with Mercedes the notable exception.

Allison and his engineers instead chose to begin the season with a car that was already relatively mature. Its aerodynamic and mechanical solutions were not simply initial specifications awaiting substantial refinement, but designs that had effectively undergone much of their development before the opening race.

This allowed Mercedes to concentrate primarily on optimising its power unit and, importantly, establish a clearer picture of the advantage it held over the competition.

There was, of course, no absolute guarantee that the Mercedes power unit would immediately become the benchmark. However, the team wanted to eliminate potential distractions, particularly the uncertainty associated with a chassis that was difficult to set up.

It was therefore essential that the relationship between the chassis and aerodynamic package was already well understood, thoroughly validated and capable of delivering the required performance.

[Article continues below]

The W17's floor remained largely unchanged for much of the season, thanks to a highly refined and effective design that had already been established during pre-season testing.

Why the W17 played to Antonelli's strengths

Mercedes' development philosophy had two significant consequences for its drivers.

First, they needed to focus heavily on optimising the use of the power unit, particularly its electrical energy deployment.

Second, they had to adapt their driving styles to the car's existing aerodynamic and mechanical characteristics, knowing that major upgrades capable of fundamentally changing its behaviour were unlikely to arrive in the short term.

The combination of those demands highlighted Antonelli's exceptional qualities while also exposing some of the limitations of his team-mate, George Russell, despite the Briton's unquestionable speed and competitiveness.

With the exception of occasional standout performances from Russell, it was Antonelli who consistently transformed the W17 into a car capable of delivering lap times beyond the reach of its rivals.

A major part of that advantage came from the Mercedes power unit, which remains ahead of the competition, particularly in its management and deployment of electrical energy.

Antonelli proved remarkably adept at exploiting those characteristics.

Working closely with race engineer Peter Bonnington, better known as 'Bono', the Italian developed an almost entirely counter-intuitive driving style that allowed him to extract the maximum available performance with extraordinary consistency.

His ability to adapt to the demands of the power unit, without compromising the car's overall balance, became one of the defining factors in his championship success.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The W17's aerodynamic strengths – and hidden weaknesses

Although the Mercedes chassis and aerodynamic package were not necessarily the outright class leaders in every area, neither represented a significant weakness.

Indeed, both contributed important strengths to the W17's overall performance.

From a mechanical perspective, the chassis provided a relatively straightforward platform for establishing an effective set-up, allowing the tyres to operate within their ideal performance windows in most conditions.

Aerodynamically, the W17 combined strong efficiency with a well-balanced distribution of downforce.

It did not necessarily generate the highest absolute levels of downforce on the grid, but the way that load was distributed across the car proved particularly effective.

That balance helped make the W17 an exceptionally competitive package, even if extracting its ultimate potential required a highly specific driving approach.

The limitations of the original concept became more apparent when Mercedes introduced its first major aerodynamic upgrade package of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The changes centred on a revised floor and reshaped sidepods, but integrating the new components with the existing car proved more difficult than anticipated.

The upgrade package was only fully completed in Austin, where Mercedes introduced a new front wing.

That component had been set aside at the previous two events because of the difficulties encountered in making the earlier aerodynamic changes work as intended.

The experience demonstrated just how finely balanced the W17's original configuration had been, and why Mercedes had been reluctant to pursue the continuous development programme favoured by its rivals.

[Article continues below]

The bargeboards, the aerodynamic deflectors positioned ahead of the sidepods, were the only components to undergo substantial development before the major upgrade package introduced in Malaysia.

Mercedes introduced a revised specification in Montreal, designed to improve pressure management around the floor and optimise its aerodynamic performance.

How Antonelli unlocked the W17's full potential

Ultimately, the W17 proved to be a car with very few weaknesses, most of which were cleverly concealed by the strength of its overall package.

But that did not make it an easy car to drive at the limit.

Its performance depended on a precise combination of aerodynamic balance, mechanical set-up and, above all, intelligent management of the power unit's electrical energy.

While Russell was occasionally able to unlock that potential, Antonelli demonstrated an exceptional ability to do so consistently.

The Italian's achievement was therefore about considerably more than simply having the fastest car.

Mercedes provided him with an outstanding technical platform, but it was Antonelli's understanding of its characteristics, adaptability and unconventional driving technique that allowed him to make the difference.

The W17 may not have been a perfect Formula 1 car. In Antonelli's hands, however, it became the perfect championship-winning weapon.

And the 20-year-old mastered it.

title: Astonishing Lewis Hamilton comeback triggers Max Verstappen title worry
excerpt:
In one of the most intense seasons in F1 history, the Sao Paulo Grand Prix in 2021 marked yet another flashpoint between Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen.

Lewis Hamilton completed one of the most dramatic comeback victories of his career at the 2021 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, winning from 10th on the grid after a weekend that began with disqualification and punishment.

Hamilton was thrown out of Friday qualifying after his Mercedes failed a DRS deflection test, with stewards finding the rear wing's outer flap opened beyond the permitted 85 millimetres under Article 3.6.3 of the technical regulations.

The stewards accepted the failure likely stemmed from a mechanical fault rather than deliberate design, but strict liability rules meant disqualification was unavoidable.

That dropped him to the back of the grid for Saturday's sprint, where he also carried a separate five-place grid penalty for an additional internal combustion engine, applied to Sunday's race.

Hamilton's blistering pace was already on display during the sprint, as he climbed 15 positions in 24 laps to end the sprint in fifth.

Starting the grand prix down in 10th, Hamilton sliced through the field and set up a fierce fight for the lead with Max Verstappen, who had started second, behind pole-sitter Valtteri Bottas.

The Dutchman held firm in a lengthy defensive battle, resisting the Mercedes for much of the race before Hamilton finally found a way past.

The seven-time champion went on to win by over 10 seconds from Verstappen, with Valtteri Bottas completing the podium, cutting further into the championship leader's advantage.

What was said after the race?

Hamilton reflected on the scale of the turnaround in the press conference afterwards.

"Coming into this weekend I never, ever thought that we would be able to close the gap like we have today," he said, speaking to the FIA press conference. "These things that just kept going against us, but I think it shows for everyone, just never give up."

"It's easy to get down when you are faced with difficult things like penalties and engine penalties. But everyone just stayed positive, everyone has done such a great job."

Verstappen, who defended for much of the race distance, was pragmatic about losing out at the front.

"We tried everything we could of course," he said.

"It was a good battle but of course at the end we just missed a little bit of pace. But we gave it all today and it was a lot of fun."

"We still have a good points lead you know, so today was a bit of damage limitation on a weekend where it was a bit difficult but I'm confident that in the coming races we'll bounce back."

title: Lando Norris praises 'insane' Kimi Antonelli: 'That's an understatement'
excerpt:
Lando Norris has lauded new F1 drivers' champion Kimi Antonelli after the Mercedes driver secured the 2026 title.

Norris was crowned at last year's season finale and will relinquish the #1 at the end of the current campaign.

Whilst the McLaren driver has endured a torrid title defence, through no real fault of his own, he was keen to congratulate Antonelli.

"He deserves it," Norris told Sky Sports F1 after the Mexico City Grand Prix. "He has been insane this year — and that's an understatement.

"Congrats to him. Especially at his age. Twenty is incredibly impressive."

Antonelli smashed Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest champion in F1 history by over three years, and joins exclusive company as one of three drivers to win the title in just their second season — excluding Juan Manuel Fangio, who took the crown in the championship's second campaign in 1951 — after Jacques Villeneuve and Lewis Hamilton, in 1997 and 2008, respectively.

Norris expressed his joy at seeing Antonelli conquer F1, a feeling that is widely shared in the paddock with the Italian a near-universally popular champion.

"So I'm very, very happy for him; he's a lovely, lovely guy," the 26-year-old said.

"He deserves it an incredible amount, and I hope even though he's young, he goes out and celebrates it properly!

"He has done an outstanding season, so very happy for him."

title: 'Broken' George Russell defended for unauthorised F1 absence: 'It was a step too far'
excerpt:
Martin Brundle has supported George Russell skipping his FIA-mandated media duties after Kimi Antonelli clinched the F1 drivers' championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Russell missed the usual post-race press pen at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez after his Mercedes team-mate was crowned, an eventuality that has long been evident given Antonelli's healthy lead in the standings.

Brundle insisted he does not "blame" the British driver, who has slumped to fourth in the title fight, for avoiding the media, something for which Russell has received criticism, even though he made sure to congratulate Antonelli and the 20-year-old's family before departing the circuit.

Mercedes gave the eight-time grand prix winner permission, but a lack of authorisation from the motorsport governing body earned the team a €5,000 fine.

Team principal Toto Wolff appeared happy to pay, taking a sympathetic and understanding approach to a "devastated" Russell, who has endured a bruising campaign, having been comfortably beaten by Antonelli in a season he was the overwhelming favourite to take the title.

Reflecting on Russell and the championship fight, Brundle told Sky Sports News: "He'll be broken, because he waited at Williams for a long time as a Mercedes junior to get his chance in the works Mercedes team, and got it just as they stopped winning.

"They suddenly turned up with these new 2026 cars, with an early dominant car. It's not dominant right now, but it was certainly in the first phase of the season, and then this kid turns up and just transforms from a bit of a liability in year one to a generational talent in year two, and George has had to observe that, and I think it's affected his own performance.

"And then he's been so unlucky, but then Antonelli had his fair share of unreliability and dropping out races too."

[Article continues below]

Brundle backs Russell actions at his 'lowest ebb'

Brundle empathised with Russell's state of mind after the grand prix, regardless of how long-coming the outcome has been.

He highlighted the generous access the press has to F1 drivers, something that is often taken for granted, and pointed out that it was just too much, too soon for the 28-year-old.

"George didn't want to face the media straight after the race; don't blame him," the former F1 driver added.

"We get more access to Formula 1 drivers than any other sport could even dream of, with top players in, or what have you in their sports, their disciplines.

"And I think it was a step too far for George... He did congratulate him, of course, underneath the podium, but to put up with, well, 'How do you feel, George?' And, 'Is this the end of the road for you?'

"So I don't blame him. The team got fined €5000, and George will be... I would be very happy to pay that, to be honest, not to have to basically face the music to the world when I'm at my lowest ebb, and I think that's fair enough, frankly."

title: Charles Leclerc becomes a father as birth of baby announced
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has announced the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca, with his wife, Alexandra.

The Ferrari driver confirmed the news on social media, revealing that Bianca was born on Tuesday, 3 November, 2026.

The announcement was accompanied by a photograph showing the newborn's legs and feet, dressed in pink trousers and cream booties.

The arrival marks a significant personal milestone for the 29-year-old Monegasque, who married Alexandra in a private ceremony in Monaco in February this year.

The couple confirmed they were expecting their first child in August, having previously kept the pregnancy largely out of the public eye.

Leclerc had spoken about his impending fatherhood during the United States Grand Prix weekend last month, insisting he did not expect to miss a race despite the approaching birth.

However, he acknowledged that he could make adjustments to his travel schedule to spend more time with his family.

"I don't think I'll miss a race, but obviously I'll do absolutely everything to be at home as much as possible in between those races," Leclerc said at the time.

"So, I might arrive a little bit late. But I will be doing the races on Sunday."

The birth comes during a busy period in the F1 calendar, with Leclerc preparing for this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The Ferrari driver is currently fifth in the drivers' championship as the 2026 season approaches its conclusion, with four rounds remaining.

title: Charles Leclerc fires back after intense Lewis Hamilton spat
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc does not believe his race-defining clash with Lewis Hamilton on the first lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix will be "much of a talking point" internally at Ferrari.

The incident between the team-mates at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez cost them a clear shot at victory, having emerged from the opening sequence of corners first and second.

Hamilton led from pole, but when Leclerc attacked into Turn 4, the seven-time F1 drivers' champion responded by braking late. Neither made the corner.

This not only culminated in a five-second time penalty for the latter, after he cut the corner and took the lead, but it also opened the door for Max Verstappen to snatch second off the former.

The confluence of events left Leclerc unable to hand the position back to Hamilton without giving the Red Bull driver the lead.

His team-mate was angered by the situation, taking to team radio to vent his frustration in no uncertain terms, highlighting the disadvantage to his race and insisting there were "big problems" to address.

Leclerc defended the decision not to give place back to Hamilton, but did acknowledge it would be a talking point on some level.

"I didn't really have clear feedback, and I think it was just confusing enough to keep the position," he told media, including RacingNews365. "I was expecting some kind of penalty...

"I spoke briefly with the team to try to understand. I asked, 'What shall I do now?'

"It's always very tricky. And obviously, in that situation, you kind of expect to... you have to do something, but is it second? Is it third? Is it fourth? Well, fourth probably didn't make sense, but second or third.

"In the end, I kept going. Obviously, it's going to be a bit of a talking point for sure at the next briefing."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc defends himself

Verstappen took advantage when Leclerc served his punishment during the pit stop phase, taking a lead he would not relinquish despite the later Valtteri Bottas-induced red flag and second standing start.

The Monegasque driver, on the other hand, faltered and ended up finishing fourth, behind Hamilton and Kimi Antonelli, who clinched the F1 drivers' championship.

Defending his approach to the opening lap skirmish, Leclerc played down how significant the incident was, and how much time it would occupy in the next Ferrari briefing.

"We are fighting for the win, and so, of course, there's going to be very little margin left from him and from me," he stated.

"In the end, we both made a mistake going into Turn 4. It's not like we had contact or whatever. We both went straight, and that gave the opportunity for Max to overtake.

"So, I don't think it should be that much of a talking point.

"Of course, it was close; [Turns] 1-2-3 was very close, but I was expecting it to fight for the lead.

"[Turns] 4 [and] 5, we both made a mistake that I paid for with a penalty. Then you can argue whether it's enough or not, and Lewis then paid out of [Turn] 5 with Max."

title: Thunderstorms threaten in ominous 2026 F1 Sao Paulo Grand Prix weather forecast
excerpt:
Formula 1 could face a wet and unpredictable weekend at the São Paulo Grand Prix, with thunderstorms and rain forecast across all three days of running at Interlagos.

The Brazilian circuit is renowned for its changeable conditions, and the latest forecast suggests the weather could play a significant role in both qualifying and Sunday's race.

Friday is expected to begin with rain, although conditions should improve ahead of the opening practice session.

Temperatures are forecast to reach around 24°C, with overcast skies gradually giving way to sunny intervals during the afternoon. Both practice sessions could take place in largely dry conditions.

Saturday looks considerably more unsettled, with temperatures climbing to approximately 29°C before the threat of thunderstorms increases during the afternoon.

Showers are forecast around the time qualifying gets underway at 3pm local time, with the chance of precipitation reaching approximately 60-70%. Heavy rain could create difficult conditions for drivers battling for pole position, particularly if thunderstorms develop over the circuit.

For Sunday's grand prix, which begins at 2pm local time, temperatures are expected to drop sharply to around 17°C.

Rain and drizzle are forecast throughout the morning and into the afternoon, although there remains some uncertainty over whether the heaviest precipitation will arrive during the race itself.

The chance of rain around the start is approximately 40-50%, potentially creating a challenging afternoon for teams as they consider tyre strategies.

With Interlagos having produced numerous dramatic wet-weather races over the years, the combination of cooler temperatures and unpredictable showers could make Sunday's 71-lap contest particularly intriguing.

title: How Mercedes can win 2026 F1 constructors' title in Sao Paulo Grand Prix
excerpt:
With the drivers' title in the bag for Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes head to the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on the cusp of winning the constructors' title for another championship double.

As it stands, Mercedes has 630 points to nearest challenger Ferrari on 504 - a gap of 126 points heading into the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

With four rounds still planned, it means there are 172 points left on the table - with 129 remaining following the race weekend at Interlagos.

It means that for Mercedes to claim the 2026 F1 constructors' title in Brazil, it must simply outscore Ferrari by three points or more.

At the very least, if Ferrari fail to score in Sao Paulo, Antonelli or George Russell would be required to finish at least eighth - and earn four points.

For Ferrari to continue the fight to Las Vegas, it must out-score Mercedes by four or more points, meaning an eighth-place finish is the minimum required if Mercedes fail to score.

If the gap is exactly 126 points following the Sao Paulo GP, Mercedes will win on countback, with the team enjoying 12 wins to Ferrari's two at present, with the number of wins used as the first tie-breaker when points are level.

Should Mercedes win the constructors' title in 2026, it will be the team's ninth title overall - drawing level with Williams for third on the all-time list.

title: Lewis Hamilton key milestones ahead of landmark 400th F1 grand prix
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is to become just the second F1 driver to reach 400 grands prix in this weekend's Sao Paullo GP.

The seven-time champion is currently on 399 entries and starts, having never posted a Did Not Start or withdrawal from any race which he has been entered into from his debut at the 2007 Australian GP.

Indeed, the only race Hamilton has missed was the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix, set to be his 266th, when he tested positive for COVID-19 in the week before the race.

But he was not entered into the race, so he maintains a perfect record of an equal number of entries and starts.

He is to follow old rival and team-mate Fernando Alonso in reaching the quadruple century, with Alonso set for his 448th entry and 445th start at Interlagos - the place they both won their first titles in 2005 for Alonso and 2008 for Hamilton. Alonso also added the 2006 title to his CV a year later at the same venue.

From his 399 starts to date, Hamilton has recorded 106 wins, 105 poles, 70 fastest laps, 209 podiums, and 5,277.50 points, whilst leading 5,530 laps. They are all F1 records, aside from the 70 fastest laps, with the Briton now just seven fastest laps behind Michael Schumacher's tally of 77 - with the two enjoying a record-equalling seven drivers' titles.

title: Colton Herta takes second stab at overcoming crucial FIA hurdle in pursuit of F1
excerpt:
Colton Herta will get a second bite at the cherry in Brazil after Cadillac erroneously believed the American had done enough to secure his FIA Super Licence.

Colton Herta will make a second attempt to secure the final point required for his FIA Super Licence when he takes part in first practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix.

The American will replace Sergio Perez at Cadillac for FP1 at Interlagos, where he must complete at least 100km, equivalent to 24 laps, to claim the decisive 40th point needed to become eligible to race in Formula 1.

Herta had been expected to reach the threshold during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, but confusion surrounding his IndyCar results left him one point short.

The 26-year-old has already participated in five FP1 sessions this season, at the Barcelona-Catalunya, Hungarian, Italian, United States and Mexico City Grands Prix.

However, a hydraulic issue restricted him to just five laps at Monza, preventing him from completing the 100km required to earn a Super Licence point.

That missed opportunity proved costly, as successfully completing the necessary mileage in Italy would have allowed Herta to reach the 40-point threshold in Mexico.

Instead, he has accumulated four points from his five appearances, leaving him on 39 heading into the Brazilian weekend.

[Article continues below]

Cadillac confusion leaves Herta facing further hurdle

The confusion emerged in Mexico when Cadillac incorrectly believed Herta had reached the FIA-mandated threshold following his FP1 appearance.

An error on the IndyCar website had incorrectly classified Herta sixth in the 2025 standings, rather than seventh, ahead of Felix Rosenqvist.

That discrepancy meant Herta had earned four Super Licence points for his 2025 campaign, rather than the six Cadillac had initially calculated — even though the American's squad's maths was already wrong.

Combined with one point from 2023, 30 from 2024 and four from his F1 practice outings, his tally stands at 39.

Herta is fighting to secure a Cadillac race seat for 2027, despite an underwhelming Formula 2 campaign that has raised questions over his readiness for F1.

With Perez confirmed at the American outfit until the end of 2029, it is Valtteri Bottas whose seat is under threat should Cadillac decide to promote Herta.

Securing the necessary mileage at Interlagos would remove the regulatory obstacle preventing his graduation, although it would not guarantee him a place on next season's grid.

title: Lando Norris eager for F1 'rewards' as quirky McLaren trait explained
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained how he is eager for "F1 rewards" he got earlier in the season for his current high-level of driving.

Norris hit a purple patch of form from the Hungarian GP to the Spanish GP in Madrid, taking pole position at the Hungaroring, at Zandvoort, and in Madrid, converting the first two into dominant victories.

He was set for a third win in four races at the first race on the Madring after a stunning pole position, but an unfortunately timed VSC deployment meant he dropped to third place.

Since then, the MCL40 machine has proved fickle to extract performance from, with Norris being vocal about the difficulties in driving the car, which has weaknesses in slow-speed corners, on the initial corner entry, and problems with drag - in part due to shorter gear ratios - which it elected not to change in the season.

In Mexico City, Norris equalled his best result since the third in Spain after a tough triple-header across Azerbaijan-Bahrain-Singapore, having also finished fifth in the United States - although this was largely due to a Hail Mary strategy in hoping for a safety car.

In Mexico, Norris battled with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, including wheel-barging on the final lap, but ultimately could not get past.

The outgoing world champion believes he is driving at a high level, but is simply not getting the luck he did earlier in the season, as he explained how under-driving the car could actually make it go faster.

"I still feel like I'm driving well, and I still feel like I'm putting together some of my best races that I've done," Norris reflected to media, including RacingNews365, after the Mexico City race.

"It is just that in the middle part of the year, I got rewarded for it and I could win.

"Now, if I drive just as good I'm not rewarded because the car is not as quick, or it is too easy to make mistakes.

"In a race, you're kind of forced to drive a little bit more under the limit; you cannot drive it at 101% all the time, and for some reason, [performance] seems to come back to us.

"But it did [in Mexico]. If we look at Baku, I think we were still struggling for pace, so we need to improve the car at certain tracks and in certain areas a lot more.

"[Mexico] was good, but I'm not convinced that if we go back to the tracks we struggled at, we'd be good all of a sudden, so it suited us.

"But I don't want to rely on hope and luck for our performance, so we know what we need to improve on, and it just takes time."
